When I first built Bot traffic on DataFast, I made it free for everyone.

I wanted you to see when AI assistants, search engines, and other crawlers request pages on your website.

As more people started using it (~1K websites now!), processing all those requests became surprisingly expensive (mostly rate limiting and database).

To keep the feature sustainable and as affordable as possible, starting on September 15, 2026, every account gets a fresh allowance of 100,000 accepted Bot traffic requests per billing cycle.

If you need more after that, an additional 1M requests costs $9/month.

You can reduce usage by excluding crawlers you don't want to track. For instance, Meta is scraping like crazy on some websites. Use the cog icon on the bot traffic card to choose what crawlers you want to track.

90% of you guys shouldn't be impacted by this update; it's only for a few websites getting loads of crawlers.

If you reach the limit, don't worry: your dashboard stays available and your regular web analytics keeps tracking normally. We only stop recording new Bot traffic until your next billing-cycle reset, unless you add more capacity.

Thanks for understanding and for using DataFast ❤️

text:
Should you eat organic food or not?

@bryan_johnson said that sometimes organic is worse than non-organic, so I wanted to check this myself.

I found 2 datasets:

- 🇺🇸 California DPR: 330 organic + 2,743 non-organic samples
- 🇩🇪 EFSA Germany: 1,913 organic + 7,907 non-organic samples

I compared measured pesticide concentrations, detection frequency, multiple residues, and EPA-relative exposure.

1. Pesticide residues appeared in 13.9% organic vs 75.2% non-organic, about 82% less often.
2. Organic had lower EPA-relative exposure for 22 of 23 foods.

I plotted the chart below that shows organic foods in color and their non-organic equivalents in gray for comparison: https://t.co/lqryeeY98u

What I understand from this data:

1) If you can, go full organic.
2) If not, prioritize organic for 🥬 lettuce (5% vs 80% detected), 🍎 apples (5% vs 91%), 🫑 peppers (16% vs 80%), 🍐 pears (22% vs 89%), and 🥬 spinach (31% vs 95%).
3) Broccoli 🥦 is a lower priority: exposure was only 0.014% vs 0.022% of the EPA reference level

I spent 14 days in China, and it was my favorite trip in a while.

It changed so much since I visited 11 years ago that it felt like a new country. Here is what I liked about China, and what I didn’t.

1. EV adoption is huge. 100% of scooters are electric. You can walk on busy streets and it’s surprisingly quiet! It made me enjoy cities again.

2. It’s so convenient. All restaurants let you scan a QR code to order and pay. You can order a taxi and drive 100 km for $30. The malls are so big you can spend an entire day there.

3. Value for money is top notch. Hotels are new, food is delicious, and yet everything is super affordable. Chinese people are really committed to doing their best, and you can feel this everywhere you go. It’s very humbling.

4. Chinese people are super friendly! We made friends everywhere we went: restaurants, hotels, taxis. I memorized Chinese sentences like 是免費的嗎？ (“Is it free?”) and I would repeat them to outdoor vendors for fun. They would laugh and come slap me on the shoulder! I even got a free ice cream doing this ^^

5. Internet is a gamble. The Great Firewall blocks a lot of websites. You need a VPN and eSIM to access Western websites. And it’s not guaranteed to work, so it’s tricky to get deep work done. I used Revolut eSIMs. It’s expensive, but most websites worked.

When I called my parents during the trip, they couldn’t believe how modern China is. For most people in the West, China is still a third-world country.

There are 17 cities with 10M+ inhabitants. Most of them were built in the last 30 years.

When I was in Hangzhou 杭州, I felt like I was in an ant house. Very crowded, yet super modern, quiet, and organized.

My wife and I loved the trip so much. We’ll come back next year and get lost in China because there are so many wonderful places to go.

quotedPost.text:
At yesterday's meetup I asked Marc why he's never shipped an AI wrapper 😅

His two most profitable products have almost nothing to do with AI. Everyone else is chasing the AI hype. He just doesn't.

His answer had two parts.

1. he builds things he wants to use himself every day.

2. he asks what still won't be replaceable by AI in 5 or 10 years. His example was TrustMRR. Real buyers and real sellers who trust the place. An AI wrapper can die the day OpenAI ships one new feature. But nobody ships a feature that takes your buyers and sellers away.

So you pick the niche, and you don't chase whatever is hot this month. With AI there's a new hype almost every single month. You pick, and then you wait. The compounding only shows up years later. And if you don't actually love the thing, you won't stay long enough to see it.

There's a word going around in China right now, OPC, one person company. Everyone wants to build one, and with AI making everything fast and easy, everyone wants one that prints money fast.

Marc told us he wanted to build a social network early on, right after watching The Social Network. He wanted to get rich. Everyone starts there 🤪

We're both just normal people, zero followers, zero products, no idea how to get users. Honestly we still think about that last part every day.

If you're starting one of these, pick something you like and are already a bit good at. Ship one feature in your MVP. See if anyone wants it. If they do, stay on it and listen to the people using it.

Then go tell the story yourself and build your own flywheel.

text:
I got a haircut in China.

Normally, I go to $5 local barbershops in Bali, but I wanted to try a hair salon in Shanghai.

I had to choose the level of expertise of the hairdresser. I was in a hurry, so I picked the only one available: Intermediate.

I Googled “men haircut 2026” and showed him one I liked.

He said nothing, washed my hair, and picked up a shaver.

45 minutes later, I realized I had a massage appointment. I felt terrible because I had to leave the salon. I looked like a palm tree.

When I came back the next day, I offered to pay for a second haircut. He refused. I insisted, but he wouldn’t let me, so I got him a croissant.

He spent the next hour finishing the haircut. He cared about every detail. He didn’t stop until my hair looked exactly like the photo I showed him.

It cost $30, and it’s the best haircut I’ve ever had (imho).

What has impressed me the most in China is how seriously people take their work.

Waiters, taxi drivers, hairdressers, massage therapists… once you pay for a service, they seem genuinely committed to making sure you feel you got your money’s worth. They're not waiting for praise. They just quietly do the job as well as they can.

And I find that incredibly humbling.
